source.title: Progressive Behavioral Drift through Compression Valleys in Large Language Models
source.authors: Zhiyuan Xu; Stanislav Abaimov; Joseph Gardiner; Sana Belguith

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the single-refusal-direction study and mentions refusal-direction removal as prior work, but does not test or rely on that specific finding. Its own steering experiments use directions for other behaviors.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SSS-induced Evil behavior scores, but these are not tests of a refusal direction: SSS uses behavior-specific steering vectors rather than the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, and does not ablate or add that refusal direction. The Evil prompts are indirect behavior evaluations, not a direct test of refusal on harmful requests. Rows below are recorded as related findings that fit none of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Arditi et al. as prior work on refusal directions and weight-editing, but never extracts, ablates, or adds a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. It steers four other behaviours (Evil, Hallucination, Sycophancy, Beshift) with behaviour-specific DiM+PCA vectors built from contrastive responses, and induces those behaviours on purpose. No refusal rate is reported as an outcome. Its remark that early refusals limit Evil steering is incidental and does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that attention sinks and compression valleys form high-gain regions that SSS exploits. SSS gives strong behavioural shifts across four axes, with small coherence loss and negligible MMLU/GSM8K degradation. They also note its effect is limited for short generations and when heavily aligned models refuse early. They add that output guardrails miss 25–40% of SSS-induced harmful outputs.
record.recipe_differences: SSS extracts behavior-specific directions by combining difference-in-means and PCA, then injects them at a selected layer using BOS anchoring and adaptive token-level reinforcement. It neither uses the original refusal direction nor projects that direction out or adds it as a refusal intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: SSS's Evil steering effect depends on generation length; the paper reports early refusals as a particular limitation.

fits_no_version.finding: SSS, a progressive BOS-anchored, sensitivity-scaled steering attack, raises judged Evil scores well above benign on Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1-8B and DeepSeek-R1-7B. It barely moves GPT-OSS-20B, where short early refusals cut generation short. CAA beats SSS on Evil (48.0 vs 41.4 average).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behaviour-specific activation steering can induce malicious outputs, and strongly aligned models resist progressive steering through early refusal termination.

record.problems: The paper does not directly measure refusal-direction intervention or refusal rates. Evil behavior is deliberately induced by steering, and Evil prompts are indirect rather than direct harmful instructions. Main reported scores have no stated error bars or confidence intervals; the authors also identify short generations and early refusals as limiting the attack.
record.rows_left_out: Other SSS target behaviors, steering baselines, coherence scores, and general-capability benchmark scores were omitted because they do not test the refusal direction or its predicted removal/addition effects.

untested.parts: No refusal direction extracted. No ablation, addition, or capability check for such a direction.
SSS is not analysed as suppressing a refusal direction. No adversarial training.
No transfer across languages or model variants.
Reasoning models are steered on other behaviours, but V1 is not tested in them.

record.verdict_notes: Every row is an induced-behaviour steering result unrelated to the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. The record's classification (cites_only, T6, no versions) is correct. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No refusal-direction measurement, ablation, addition, or assessment of general capability after intervening on that direction.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
SSS is not tested as suppression of the refusal direction, and no training against its ablation is evaluated.
No comparison of single versus multiple refusal directions, affine structure, or a refusal cone.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision is tested.
No transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages is tested.
No comparison of refusal training procedures or training stages for direction removability.
Some evaluated models use chain-of-thought, but the study does not test the refusal-direction claim in reasoning models.
